study.title: Malachi 3 - Purification, Repentance and Final distinction
study.overview: Malachi 3 presents a response from God to the complaints and infidelity of the people. The chapter begins with the promise of the coming of the messenger who prepares the way and of the Lord himself who comes to his temple to purify, judge and restore the covenant. Then God calls the people to repentance, denouncing both the breaking of the cultual fidelity and the hardness of the words against him. The chapter ends with the hope that in the time of God the difference between those who fear him will be evident and what is indifferent to him.

outline.title: The coming of the messenger and the purifying fire
outline.explanation: God announces that he will send his messenger to prepare the way, and that the Lord will come to his temple. This coming is not only comfort: it is also examination, purification and judgment. The focus lies on the children of Levi, who will be refined so that the offering will be pleasing again; at the same time, God presents himself as the one who judges practices of sin and oppression, showing that his constancy is the reason that the people have not been consumed.

outline.title: Called to return and accusation of theft
outline.explanation: God accuses the people of old detachment from their laws and call: "Return to me, and I will turn to you." The nation's answer reveals spiritual blindness, because it asks how it should return. The text then identifies a concrete sin: retaining tithes and offerings, which is described as robbery against God. The promise, linked to obedience, is of provision, protection against the devourer and recognition among the nations.

outline.title: Hard words, perseverance of those who fear and final verdict
outline.explanation: The people speak with arrogance and skepticism, saying that serving God is useless, while the proud seem to prosper. In contrast, those who fear the Lord talk to each other and are remembered before him; their names are recorded as those of their special property. The chapter closes with the promise that a time will come when the difference between the righteous and the wicked will be clear, both among those who serve God and among those who do not serve him.

study.context: The chapter reflects a community that lives with formal cult, practical infidelity and spiritual discouragement. The text itself shows a style of debate in which the Lord accuses and the people answer defensive questions. The notes provided also relate the proclamation of the messenger to the preparation for the coming of the Messiah, and see the closing of the chapter as a statement that God will do justice and publicly distinguish the two ways.
study.theology: Malachi 3 teaches that the coming of God is not neutral: it purifies its people and judges evil. The Lord is holy and constant; therefore, his covenant does not tolerate hypocritical worship or social injustice. Repentance here is not mere remorse, but a return of loyalty and direction of life. The financial infidelity in worship is treated as unfaithfulness to God, showing that worship and obedience cannot be separated. Finally, the chapter states that the apparent advantage of the wicked is temporary; God preserves those who fear it, and at the right time will make visible the distinction between the two groups.

scholarViews.insight: The Messenger is understood as a envoy who prepares the way for divine coming; the note also notes that Christian tradition saw here Jesus as the messenger of the new covenant, which illuminates the Messianic expectation of the verse.
The call "Return to me," and I will turn to you, is explained as an urgent invitation to repentance and a real change of direction, within the covenant relationship between God and his people.
The final verse is read as the moment when the difference between the righteous and the wicked will be clearly manifest, and in which one will see who really served God.

questions: In which areas of my life can I be saying, like the people, that I am close to God, but in practice I have moved away from their ways?
How does my contribution to worship, service and generosity reveal trust in God or resistance to him?
If God has recorded those who fear him, my words and attitudes show that I belong to this group?
study.practice: This chapter calls to examine one's own fidelity seriously. Concrete application can begin with three steps: confess areas of disobedience without excuses; order financial and ministerial life honestly before God; and to persevere in talking to others who fear the Lord, rather than uniting with cynicism. It is also worth remembering that the sense of injustice present in the present is not the last word: God sees, records and judges with righteousness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided associate the messenger of 3:1 with John the Baptist and, in a Christian way, to Christ as a messenger of the new covenant; this is an interpretative reading, not something explicitly said by the text of Malachi. There is also no safe data in the notes to detail specific calendar, geography or historical circumstances beyond the general picture of the people's cultural and moral infidelity.
